claims.text: A tungsten-based host alloy can contain SRO identified as SrRuO3 precipitates.
Directional solidification of the proposed tungsten-based alloy produces a large-grained microstructure.
Directional solidification promotes coarsening and spatial isolation of SrRuO3 precipitates in the tungsten host.
The initial tungsten-based alloy has a fine-grained matrix containing uniformly distributed SrRuO3 precipitates.
High-temperature regimes exist in which phonon conduction dominates heat transport in the proposed tungsten-based alloy.
Controlled grain growth can be achieved in this system without introducing excessive defects.
Coarsening and spatial separation of SrRuO3 precipitates reduce the total precipitate–matrix interface area available for phonon scattering.
Reduced precipitate-interface scattering increases the phonon mean free path in the tungsten matrix.
An increased phonon mean free path enhances lattice-mediated heat transport.
A large-grained tungsten-based alloy with sparse, coarsened SrRuO3 precipitates has higher lattice thermal conductivity than a comparable fine-grained alloy with uniformly distributed precipitates.
At very high temperatures, other heat-transport mechanisms may complicate the proposed conductivity enhancement.
Defects introduced during processing may add scattering and complicate the proposed conductivity enhancement.
The magnitude of the conductivity improvement depends on grain growth, precipitate coarsening, and side effects of directional solidification.
Grain size and precipitate size and spacing can be compared between conventionally cast and directionally solidified samples using microscopy.
Lattice thermal conductivity can be measured by time-domain thermoreflectance under identical temperature conditions.
Failure of the directionally solidified sample to show a statistically significant conductivity increase would falsify the hypothesis.
